chapters.title: What a tick is worth
chapters.dek: Options are quoted in price and traded in volatility. The exchange rate between them varies by a factor of three hundred across a single chain.

figures.title: One cent, in vol points, across the chain
figures.caption: The curve is essentially 1/vega, and vega collapses in the wings and toward expiry — so the cost of a tick explodes exactly where options are cheapest. That inversion is why the cheapest options are the most expensive to trade.

checks.q: A weekly 5-delta call is quoted 0.05 at 0.10. Is that a wide market?
checks.right: In cents it is five ticks; in vol it is about three and a half points. Convert before judging, and expect it to be wide because the tick will not permit tighter
checks.why: Convert it to vol first. Five cents on an option with a vega of roughly 0.014 per point is about 3.5 vol points, which sounds wide and is only a few ticks from the tightest market the grid allows — a single penny on that vega is still 0.7 of a vol point, twenty times what it is on a six-month at-the-money option, and further out the wing it runs to tens of points. The percentage-of-premium framing is the least useful one available, because the denominator is tiny by construction. The last answer is not wrong that delta matters, but it is vega, not delta, that sets the conversion.

chapters.text: A market maker thinks in volatility. The screen shows price. The conversion between them is vega, and because vega varies enormously across a chain while the tick size does not, the same one-cent increment means completely different things at different strikes . On a six-month at-the-money option, vega is large — a cent is about 0.04 vol points , an amount too small to care about. On a seven-day five-delta option, vega is tiny, and that same cent is 0.70 vol points . A nickel-wide market is 0.2 vol wide in the first case and 3.5 vol wide in the second. This single table explains a set of things that otherwise look like separate facts. Why far out-of-the-money short-dated markets appear absurdly wide in percentage terms. Why you cannot quote them tightly even if you want to — the tick will not let you. Why a market maker will happily show a penny market in one option and refuse to show anything reasonable in another on the same underlying. And why an "edge" of two cents is meaningless until you know which option it was in. The practical version: before reacting to a quoted spread, convert it to vol. A market that looks scandalous in cents is often unremarkable in vol, and occasionally the reverse. One cent, in vol points, across the chain The same market width, priced two ways Chain The curve is essentially 1/vega, and vega collapses in the wings and toward expiry — so the cost of a tick explodes exactly where options are cheapest. That inversion is why the cheapest options are the most expensive to trade. Derivation — why one tick is worth twenty times more on one option than another A quoted price and a quoted volatility are the same information in different units. The exchange rate between them is vega. [equation: Δσ = Δprice / vega] Reads as: to convert a price move into a volatility move, divide by how much the option's price changes per volatility point. Everything about this chapter is that one division. So the volatility value of a fixed tick is not a property of the tick. It is a property of the denominator, and vega collapses in exactly the situations where the tick does not. [equation: vega = S·e^−qT·n(d_1)·√T] Reads as: vega is large when there is time left and the option is near the money, and vanishes otherwise. The √T kills short expiries; the n(d₁) kills far strikes. Both factors shrink together on a short-dated out-of-the-money option, so the denominator becomes tiny while the numerator stays fixed at one cent. That is the whole explanation for the 0.04-versus-0.70 figure in the table: the numerator never changed. Where it breaks. The conversion assumes there is an implied volatility to move — that the quoted price sits inside the no-arbitrage bounds and the option has enough value to invert. On the deepest, shortest options the price is essentially all intrinsic and the implied volatility is barely identified, so a one-tick move can imply an enormous volatility change or none at all depending on rounding. At that point the vol quote is an artefact of the price grid rather than a measurement, which is why desks stop quoting those series in volatility and start quoting them in cents. Try this Set the expiry to seven days and drag the strike far out of the money. Predict roughly how many volatility points one cent is worth before you read it — most people are out by a factor of ten.

chapters.title: What is actually inside a spread
chapters.dek: Four components, and only one of them is profit.

figures.title: Decomposition of a quoted half-spread
figures.caption: The components are illustrative weights rather than measured ones — no desk publishes this decomposition. What is not illustrative is the ordering: on most options, edge is the smallest term, which is why market making is a volume business and why a small change in fees or hedging cost moves quoted spreads visibly.

chapters.text: A quoted market is not a fee. It is the sum of several distinct costs the market maker faces, plus whatever is left over. Hedging cost. Take the other side of an option and you immediately need delta in the underlying, which means crossing another spread. That cost scales with the option's delta and with how liquid the stock is. Inventory risk. Having taken the position you now hold vega and gamma you did not choose, possibly for days. The wider the position's risk, the more you need paying to warehouse it. Adverse selection. Some of the people trading with you know more than you do, and they systematically trade when your quote is wrong. This is not a possibility to be insured against but a certainty to be priced, and it is chapter 03's subject. Fees. Exchange, clearing and regulatory charges, small per contract and not small in aggregate. What remains is edge. Move the sliders and notice how rarely it is the largest component — and that in the wings, where markets look widest, hedging and inventory dominate while edge is often thinner than in the tight at-the-money market next to it. Decomposition of a quoted half-spread Across the chain Conditions The components are illustrative weights rather than measured ones — no desk publishes this decomposition. What is not illustrative is the ordering: on most options, edge is the smallest term, which is why market making is a volume business and why a small change in fees or hedging cost moves quoted spreads visibly. Try this Take toxicity to zero — imagine a market with no informed traders at all. Predict whether the spread collapses to nothing, and if not, what is left.

chapters.title: Quote a market yourself
chapters.dek: Set a width. Get filled. Then look at who filled you and what happened next.

figures.title: P&L against how tight you quote
figures.caption: Push the informed share up and the whole curve sinks — at high enough toxicity there is no width that makes money, which is precisely the state a market maker withdraws in. "The market went wide" is usually this, not a preference.

figures.title: Make the market, trade by trade
figures.caption: Averaged over 300 sessions, a one-cent half-spread loses $61, because informed traders are 22.6% of its fills; at twelve cents they are 3.0% and the session averages $514, the best width here. Wider than the fifteen cents customers will tolerate and the flow dries up, leaving only the traders who know a jump is coming. Leaning your quotes a cent per hundred shares of inventory gives up some of the average, $514 to $441, and more than halves the swing from session to session, $329 to $145.

checks.q: You widen your quotes to reduce adverse selection. What happens to the share of your fills that are informed?
checks.right: It rises. Informed traders are the last to be deterred, since they only trade when their edge exceeds your spread
checks.why: It rises. Widening deters the uninformed first — they are trading for reasons unrelated to your quote's accuracy, so a worse price simply sends them elsewhere. The informed only ever traded when they had an edge, and a wider spread merely raises the bar on how large that edge must be. So the flow you retain gets more toxic even as it gets less harmful in aggregate. The right conclusion is that widening manages the size of the problem, never its composition.

terms.Adverse selection: The cost of being filled by someone who knew more than you. It is not a fee — it is the systematic tendency of your fills to happen just before the price moves against you.

chapters.text: Adverse selection is usually defined and rarely felt. Here it is a number you can move. You quote a two-sided market some number of vol points wide around your fair value. Flow arrives. Uninformed traders hit your quote because they want the option — the tighter you are, the more of them you win. Informed traders only trade when your quote is wrong by more than their edge, which means every fill from them is a fill you did not want. Quote too tight and the arithmetic is brutal. At a 0.20 vol-point half-width you get filled on 321 of 400 arrivals and lose 30.8 — you are winning enormous volume and most of the volume that matters is picking you off. Widen and volume collapses while P&L per fill climbs; at 3.50 wide you make 2.38 per fill and only trade six times. These are expected values; the figure averages 500 simulated sessions and lands within a few tenths of them. The optimum sits in between, around 1.2 vol points in these settings, and it is the same shape as page 13's execution problem viewed from the other side of the trade — a quantity you want more of, against a cost that grows with getting it. Watch the informed percentage column as you widen. It rises : informed traders are the last to be deterred, because they only trade when they have an edge big enough to cross your spread. You cannot widen your way out of adverse selection , only price it. P&L against how tight you quote At your chosen width Your market Push the informed share up and the whole curve sinks — at high enough toxicity there is no width that makes money, which is precisely the state a market maker withdraws in. "The market went wide" is usually this, not a preference. Try this Quote absurdly tight — a tenth of a volatility point — and predict whether you make money on volume. Then widen until you barely trade. The figure above runs whole days at once. Now quote one yourself, trade by trade. Somewhere behind the screen is a true value that drifts and sometimes jumps; three traders in ten know where it is going. You set how wide to quote and how far to lean your quotes against your inventory, and you can change both mid-session. Green fills came from customers; red ones came from someone who knew more than you. Make the market, trade by trade Your quotes Averaged over 300 sessions, a one-cent half-spread loses $61, because informed traders are 22.6% of its fills; at twelve cents they are 3.0% and the session averages $514, the best width here. Wider than the fifteen cents customers will tolerate and the flow dries up, leaving only the traders who know a jump is coming. Leaning your quotes a cent per hundred shares of inventory gives up some of the average, $514 to $441, and more than halves the swing from session to session, $329 to $145. Trader's lens A market maker prices two things into every spread: the cost of trading with someone who knows more, and the risk of the inventory left behind. They widen when the flow looks informed, after news or before a print, and they skew rather than widen when inventory builds, because a skewed quote invites the trade that flattens the book. Tight markets attract volume and the traders you least want; wide ones attract nobody. Watch which fills move against you right after: that is the informed share, and it sets the spread. Skew is cheaper than hedging: let the next customer take your inventory off you. Rule of thumb: if most of your fills lose money a minute later, your quotes are too tight for this flow.

chapters.title: Where the liquidity actually is
chapters.dek: Volume and open interest answer different questions, and the chain is far more concentrated than it looks.

figures.title: A typical concentration profile
figures.caption: Illustrative shapes, but the concentration is real and it is stronger than most people expect: the top handful of strikes routinely carry the majority of a chain's open interest, which is what makes the pinning mechanism in chapter 06 possible at all.

terms.Pinning: A stock finishing unusually close to a strike on expiration. One mechanism is dealers hedging a long gamma position, which mechanically buys weakness and sells strength.

chapters.text: A chain shows hundreds of lines. A small fraction of them carry nearly all the risk. Volume is what traded today — a flow measure, and it resets every session. Open interest is what remains outstanding — a stock measure, and it tells you where positions actually sit. A line with heavy volume and no open interest is day-trading churn; a line with low volume and enormous open interest is where somebody's risk lives, and it is the one that matters on expiration. Liquidity concentrates in front-month, near-the-money strikes, and falls away fast in both directions. The practical consequences: anything you want to trade in size should be checked against open interest before you assume you can get out, a "cheap" far-dated wing option may be cheap because nobody will ever bid for it again, and the greeks you compute on an illiquid line are theoretical in a way the greeks on the ATM line are not. The one that catches people: you can put on a position you cannot take off. Establishing a wing position by paying up is easy; exiting requires somebody to want the other side, and in the wings there frequently isn't one at any price you would accept. A typical concentration profile Chain shape Illustrative shapes, but the concentration is real and it is stronger than most people expect: the top handful of strikes routinely carry the majority of a chain's open interest, which is what makes the pinning mechanism in chapter 06 possible at all. Try this Concentrate the open interest hard into the front month and predict what happens to everything outside it.

chapters.title: Dealer gamma, with the condition attached
chapters.dek: The mechanism is real. It is almost always stated without the assumption it depends on.

figures.title: Terminal distance from the strike, three regimes
figures.caption: Drag impact to zero and the three distributions collapse onto each other. That is the honest headline: dealer gamma is a mechanism with a threshold, and whether any particular market is above the threshold is a question about volumes rather than about options.

checks.q: Someone argues that large dealer long gamma will suppress volatility this week. What is the missing piece of the claim?
checks.right: Whether the resulting hedging flow is large relative to normal volume. Below a threshold the effect is undetectable, and the positioning itself is inferred rather than observed
checks.why: The flow has to be big enough to matter. The hedging behavior is real and its direction is correctly described, but the price effect is the product of that flow and the market's price impact — and if the gamma is small relative to a day's volume, the product is indistinguishable from zero. That is exactly what the simulation shows at low impact. Add that dealer positioning is estimated from trade-side inference and you have two places for a confident-sounding claim to be quietly wrong.

chapters.text: The story goes: dealers are long gamma, so they sell rallies and buy dips to stay hedged, which dampens the market. Or they are short gamma, so they buy rallies and sell dips, which amplifies it. Both halves of that are correct as descriptions of hedging behavior. What is usually left out is that hedging flow only moves the market if it is large relative to everything else trading . That is a condition, it is quantitative, and it is frequently not met. The simulation makes the dependence explicit by putting price impact on a slider. At low impact the three cases — no hedging, long-gamma dealers, short-gamma dealers — are statistically indistinguishable. My first attempt at this figure used an impact coefficient small enough that the effect vanished entirely into the noise, and that failure is worth more than the eventual success: the mechanism is real and its magnitude is an empirical question with a frequently unimpressive answer. At the impact the figure opens with, the textbook result appears cleanly. Long-gamma dealers pull spot toward the strike — mean distance falls from 2.58 to 1.73 , and the share finishing within fifty cents roughly doubles, from 11.8% to 24.9% . Short-gamma dealers push it away: mean distance 3.57 , with only 3.9% finishing near the strike. Those are the opening run; press for another and each moves by a few percent, but the ordering never changes. Two honest caveats to carry alongside any dealer-positioning argument. Positioning is inferred, not observed — nobody publishes net dealer gamma, and the estimates rest on assumptions about who initiated each trade. And the flows compete with everything else in the market, so the same nominal gamma matters enormously on a quiet expiration Friday in a single name and not at all on a heavy day in an index. Terminal distance from the strike, three regimes Effect size against the impact assumption Assumptions Drag impact to zero and the three distributions collapse onto each other. That is the honest headline: dealer gamma is a mechanism with a threshold, and whether any particular market is above the threshold is a question about volumes rather than about options. Try this Drop the price impact toward zero, keeping dealer gamma large. Predict whether pinning survives on positioning alone.

chapters.title: Expiration
chapters.dek: The one day when open interest, gamma and a fixed deadline all point at the same price.

figures.title: Sample paths into the close, with and without hedging flow
figures.caption: The pinned paths are not dragged to the strike so much as slowed down near it — the hedging flow acts as friction rather than as an attractor. That distinction matters: it means the effect shows up as a change in the distribution's shape rather than as a force you could trade against directly.

chapters.text: Everything in this page compounds on expiration day. Gamma is at its maximum, so hedging flows per unit of price move are at their largest. Open interest is concentrated at round strikes. And the deadline is absolute — whatever is unhedged at the close is a decision, not a position. Pinning is the observable result, and the mechanism is chapter 05's with the dial turned up. But two other things happen that are worth knowing separately. Delta discontinuity. An option's delta at expiry is a step function, so a stock oscillating around a heavily-owned strike hands hedgers alternating large buy and sell orders. That is what makes the last hour at a pinned strike look strange. The exercise decision. Near the money at the close, whether a contract is exercised stops being automatic and becomes a judgement about where the stock will open. This is where page 03's assignment mechanics and page 04's early-exercise arithmetic meet the microstructure — and it is the reason expiration is an operations problem as much as a trading one. The practical stance: treat a large open-interest strike as a place where the price is more likely to spend the last session than a random walk would suggest, and treat that tendency as a weak statistical regularity rather than a reliable trade. The effect is real, measurable, and much smaller than the confidence with which it is usually discussed. Sample paths into the close, with and without hedging flow Expiration day The pinned paths are not dragged to the strike so much as slowed down near it — the hedging flow acts as friction rather than as an attractor. That distinction matters: it means the effect shows up as a change in the distribution's shape rather than as a force you could trade against directly.

chapters.title: What a market maker's day actually optimizes
chapters.dek: Not the direction of the stock. Inventory, and the price of being wrong about it.

figures.title: One day of inventory, with and without skewing
figures.caption: The lower panel is the trade-off, and the two ends of it are both bad. At zero aversion you capture the most spread and go home with a position whose overnight risk dwarfs it. At high aversion your inventory is beautifully flat and you have barely traded. The desk lives in the middle, and where exactly depends on how much capital is behind it.

checks.q: A market maker's quote drops a tick with no trade in the underlying and no news. What is the most likely explanation?
checks.right: Their inventory changed. Quotes carry a skew proportional to position, so the mid moves when the maker's book moves — with no view about value at all
checks.why: Their inventory changed. The observed mid is fair value plus a position adjustment, and the adjustment is invisible from outside. Treating every quote move as information is how people end up chasing a market that is only trying to go home flat — and it is the reason a single maker's mid is a worse estimate of fair value than the consensus across several.

chapters.text: The popular picture of a market maker is someone with a view who trades on it. The real job is closer to the opposite: quote both sides, try to end the day with as little position as possible, and get paid the spread for the service. The optimisation is over inventory , not over price. That changes what the quotes are for. A market maker who is long too much does not simply hedge and carry on — they skew : they move both bid and offer down, so that selling becomes more likely and buying less likely, and the position drifts back toward flat on its own. The skew is the inventory control, and it is why the mid-price you observe is not the market maker's estimate of fair value. It is fair value plus a position adjustment you cannot see. Three consequences follow, and each explains something that looks irrational from outside. The quote moves when nothing happened. A market can reprice by a tick with no trade in the underlying and no news, because someone's inventory changed. Reading that as information is a mistake, and it is a common one. Size is priced separately from price. The quote you see is for the quoted size. Asking for ten times that is a different trade with a different price, because it moves the maker's inventory ten times as far and the skew has to pay for it. Widening is a position statement. A maker who has been picked off repeatedly on one side widens that side specifically. An asymmetric market is usually a maker telling you what they already own. The figure runs a day. Orders arrive, the maker quotes with a skew proportional to inventory, and the position wanders. Turn the inventory aversion up and the position hugs zero while the spread capture falls, because skewing away from the market costs you fills. Turn it down and you capture more spread and end the day with a position you did not choose — and the P&L standard deviation, which is the number a risk manager cares about, grows with it. The result is the same shape as page 13's U-curve and page 14's own quoting simulation: an interior optimum between two costs that run in opposite directions. It is worth noticing how often that shape has turned up in this series, because it is what almost every real trading decision looks like once both sides of it are priced. [equation: quote mid = fair value − k · inventory] Reads as: the price you are shown is the maker's estimate of value, shifted by how much they already own. k is how aggressively they want the position gone. At zero aversion you capture the most spread and go home with a position whose overnight risk dwarfs it. At high aversion your inventory is beautifully flat and you have barely traded. The desk lives in the middle, and where exactly depends on how much capital is behind it. chapters.title: Who gets filled: allocation rules
chapters.dek: When an order arrives at a price where several people are bidding, the exchange's allocation rule decides who trades. The rule shapes how everyone quotes.

figures.title: Your fill against the size you display
figures.caption: Under price-time your fill is decided by when you arrived and showing more size buys nothing. Under pro-rata it is decided by how much you show, and showing more always buys more.

checks.q: On a pro-rata venue you quote 500 contracts but only want to trade 50. What risk are you running?
checks.right: A large order that takes out the whole price fills you for most of your 500
checks.why: A large order fills you for most of it. Pro-rata pays for displayed size on small orders and charges for it on big ones: once the incoming order is larger than the whole price, every quoter is filled in full. Queue position is the price-time concern, and customer priority applies on both.

chapters.text: Four orders rest at the same bid: a 20-lot from a public customer, a 200-lot from market maker A who arrived first, a 50-lot from market maker B, and yours. A seller hits the bid for 150. The figure fills that sell under the two families of rules US option exchanges use, and asks what your displayed size buys you under each. Your fill against the size you display The book and the order Under price-time your fill is decided by when you arrived and showing more size buys nothing. Under pro-rata it is decided by how much you show, and showing more always buys more. Both rules here fill the public customer first. Many US option exchanges give customer orders that priority at a price, as an overlay on either rule, though not every price-time venue does. That leaves 130 contracts. Price-time hands them out in order of arrival. Market maker A was first with 200, so A takes all 130 and you get nothing , whatever size you show. Had you been first, you would get your whole 100. The competition is for queue position, which is why speed matters on these venues. Pro-rata splits the 130 in proportion to displayed size among the market makers at the price. With 100 showing you get 37 ; show 1,000 and you get 104 , though you never wanted 1,000. That is the rule's known side effect: it pays to display more than you mean, so pro-rata books look deeper than they are, and a sweep that clears them can fill quoters for far more than they expected to trade. The real rules sit on top of these two: many venues give a participation entitlement to a designated or lead market maker, some allocate part pro-rata and part by time, auctions run their own allocation, and complex orders trade against a separate book with leg priority. The details differ by exchange and change; read the exchange's rulebook for the venue you trade on. What carries over is the question to ask of any of them: what does this rule pay for, time, size or status? [equation: pro-rata fill_i = ⌊ Q_left × size_i ÷ Σ size ⌋ price-time: fill in arrival order until Q_left is gone] Reads as: under pro-rata each quoter gets the share of what is left that their size is of the total size at the price, rounded down; under price-time the earliest order fills first. In both, customers at the price go first. Try this A seller sweeps for 1,000. Predict your fill under pro-rata if you are showing 400.

chapters.title: Check yourself

checks.q: One cent on a 180-day at-the-money option is 0.04 vol points. Roughly what is it on a 7-day 5-delta?
checks.right: About 0.7 volatility points, because vega has collapsed and the tick has not
checks.why: About 0.7 points — nearly twenty times more. The tick is fixed in price and wildly variable in volatility, because the conversion divides by vega and vega vanishes for short-dated far strikes.

checks.q: What is left in a bid–offer spread if no trader is informed?
checks.right: Hedge cost, inventory risk, fees and the maker's required edge. Adverse selection is one component of four, not the whole spread
checks.why: Most of it survives. Adverse selection is the component people name because it is the interesting one, but a maker still has to hedge, carry inventory, pay fees and earn something.

checks.q: You widen your quoted market. What happens to the share of your fills that are informed?
checks.right: It rises. Informed traders are the last to be deterred by a wider spread, so widening manages the size of adverse selection but never its composition
checks.why: It rises. This is the counterintuitive result from the quoting simulation: widening filters out uninformed flow first, because the informed trader's edge still clears the wider spread. You trade less and a larger fraction of what remains is against you.

checks.q: Under what condition does dealer gamma actually pin a stock?
checks.right: Only when hedging flow is large relative to normal volume — below that price-impact threshold the effect vanishes into the noise entirely
checks.why: Only above a flow-size threshold. The narrative is usually stated without this condition, and the condition is what makes it a claim rather than a story. Below it the simulated effect disappears completely.

checks.q: A stock settles one cent in the money against a strike you are short. What is the risk?
checks.right: A position-level exposure — you are assigned and short the shares over the weekend, with overnight risk hundreds of times the intrinsic exchanged
checks.why: A position, not a cent. Page 04 puts the numbers on it: $20 of intrinsic against roughly $3,800 of weekend risk on ten contracts. Expiry closes the option, not the stock position it delivers.

checks.q: Why does a market maker skew their quotes?
checks.right: To manage inventory. Moving both sides shifts the probability of buying versus selling, which pulls the position back toward flat without needing a hedge
checks.why: Inventory management. The mid you observe is fair value plus a position adjustment, which is why a maker's quote can move with no news and why asking for size is a different trade from the one on the screen.
